full_judgment:
3.The respondent No. 1 entered appearance and filed an affidavit-in-opposition and also a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition where from it appears that the petitioner was charge sheeted on 12.9.95 on a charge of misconduct for committing theft in the can-teen of the BDR Battalion concerned and no showed cause in due course which was not found satisfactory by the authority. Thereafter he was produced before the authority on 14.9.95 and thereafter he was issued a second show cause notice on 14.9.95 asking him to show cause why penalty of dismissal from service shall not be imposed upon him. The petitioner was heard in person and he denied the charges. After hearing the petitioner and considering the materials on record the authority found him guilty of the charges and decided to dismiss him from the service and accordingly he was given a 7 days' show cause notice to show cause why the said penalty shall not be imposed upon him along with the summary of the memo of evidence to which he replied on 20.9.95 praying for exoneration from the charges. Thereafter on 21.9.95 the petitioner was produced before the authority who considered his explanation filed in response to the second show cause notice and after hearing the petitioner passed the order of dismissal from service on 21.9.95. Thereafter release order was issued on 4.2.96 which is evidence by Annexure 'F' to the petition. The petitioner never submitted any appeal before the Sector Commander, Comilla Sector and therefore the question of refusing to accept his appeal does not arise at all. Thereafter the petitioner served a Legal Notice dated 22.4.96 in reply to which the B.D.R authority informed the petitioner to the effect that no appeal was submitted by the petitioner to the appellate authority, that is, the Sector Commandar, Comilla, and that is why they had no opportunity to consider the appeal of the petitioner. However, on receipt of the Legal Notice the Headquarters considered the same and after due consideration of the same that was rejected by the authority concerned. It is contended by the learned Assistant Attorney General that the dismissal order was passed on 21.9.95 and the said order was finally approved by the highest authority of the B.D.R. on 4.2.96 whereupon the petitioner was released from the service of the B.D.R. vide Annexure 'F' to the petition. 

 5. Ms Naima Haider, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the respondent No. 1, on the other hand, contends that it is obvious from the materials on record that the BDR authority has complied with the provisions as embodied in section 6(1) of the Ordinance in initiating the disciplinary proceeding against the petitioner and there is no claim from the side of the petitioner that there has been any violation of the provisions of section 6(i) of the Ordinance. The learned Assistant Attorney General submits that section 6(i) of the Ordinance is, no doubt, mandatory and the B.D.R. has strictly complied with the provisions thereof, namely that the petitioner was given seven days time to reply to the show cause notice. The learned Assistant Attorney General further submits that the provision of time limit as contained in sub-section (ii) of Section 6 of the said Ordinance is directory although in that sub-section the word 'shall' has been used because if the time limit as embodied by the said section is not complied with that would not cause any prejudice to the petitioner and secondly the Ordinance do not provide for any consequence for the non-compliance of the said sub-section. In support of her contention she relies on the decisions reported in A.I.R. 1980 (SC) 303, 1974 (4 S.S.C) 237, AIR 1991(ker) 240 and AIR 1973(SC) 883 and also the case of Montreal Street Railway Company Vs. Normandin reported in 1917 A.C.170 wherein it has been held that the question whether provisions in a statute are directory or mandatory has very frequently arisen before the court but no general rule can be laid down to ascertain the question whether the provisions in a statute are directory or imperative and that in every case the object of the statutes must be looked at. In support of her contention she produced all the original papers before us. 

 6. We have perused the petition along with the affidavit-in-opposition and the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition and reply thereto and the paper annexed therewith and the submissions made by the learned Advocates of the respective parties. In this case there is no dispute between the parties as to the nature of sub-section (1) of Section 6 of the Ordinance and both the learned Advocates agreed that the provisions embodied in sub-section (1) of Section 6 of the Ordinance are mandatory. It is also obvious from the materials on record that in dismissing the petitioner from the service of the BDR there has been no violation of any provisions as embodied in sub-section (1) of section 6 of the Ordinance. The only grievance and the main grievance of Mr. Shahadat Hossain is that the time limit of 20 days as embodied in sub-section (2) of Section 6 of the Ordinance is also mandatory because it is a special statute and it relates to the disciplined forces of the B.D.R. only and hence non-compliance of time limit in dismissing the petitioner has rendered the dismissal order as illegal and without jurisdiction. 

 " Now the most question is whether the provision of twenty days time limit for passing the dismissal order is mandatory or not. When the legislature itself expresses its opinion as to the consequences of non-compliance with a certain direction no difficulty arises but in a case where the legislature does not indicate its mind as to the consequence of violation of such direction, the court is to consider whether the direction is merely directory or mandatory and this is to be determined on the construction of the provision in question and the importance attached to the direction therein. 

 8. The word "shall" in its ordinary import is "obligatory", but there are many decisions wherein the courts under different situations construed the word to mean may. In the case reported in AIR 1955(SC)233 at P.245 it has been observed: 

 This passage was approved by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of State of U.P. Vs. Manbodhan Lal, 1958 SCR 533 at page 545. In Craies on Statute Law, 5th Edition, the following passage appears at p.242; 

 " This passage was accepted by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Montreal Street Rly. Co. Vs. Normandin, 1917 AC 170; AIR 1917 PC.142 and by the Indian Supreme Court in 1958 SCR 533. 

 10. The question whether a certain provision in a statute imposing a duty on a public body or authority was mandatory or only directory, arose before their Lordships of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Montreal Street Railway Company Vs Normandin. In that case the question mooted was whether the omission to revise the jury lists as directed by the statute had the effect of nullifying the verdict given by a July. Their Lordships held that the irregularities in the due revision of the Jury lists will not ipso facto avoid the verdict of a Jury. The Board made the following observation in the course of their judgment; 

 " ........The question whether provisions in a statute are directory or imperative has very frequently arisen in this country, but it has been said that no general rule can be laid down, and that in every case the object of the statute must be looked at. 

 11. We have gone through the entire Ordinance and we find that the object of the Ordinance is to maintain discipline amongst the members of the Bangladesh Rifles and there is nothing in the Ordinance indicating local would happen in the event of non-compliance of the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Ordinance. One of the criteria to determine as to whether a provision is mandatory or directory is to see whether any penalty is imposed for non-compliance of any provision of the statute. In the instant case there is nothing in the Ordinance indicating what would happen in the event of non-compliance with the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Ordinance. Moreover, non-compliance with the time limit as embodied in sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Ordinance, in our opinion, does not seriously prejudice the petitioner in any way because admittedly the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Ordinance has duly been complied with by the B.D.R. authority and on a proper enquiry the petitioner was found guilty of misconduct for which he has duly been dismissed from service on 21.9.95 and with the approval of the said order by the highest authority of the B.D.R. on 4.2.96, the petitioner was released from the service of the B.D.R. vide Annexure 'F' to the petition. It, thus, appears that in spite of offending the time limit as embodied in sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Ordinance the petitioner has not suffered any serious prejudice in view of the fact that the dismissal from service has duly been approved by the highest authority and the petitioner has been adequate opportunity to before the domestic tribunal. The time limit as in  sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Ordinance appears to us to be directory because that sub-section of the Ordinance itself enjoins upon the B.D.R. authority only to be vigilent in Concluding the disciplinary proceedings. It has been submitted by the learned Assistant Attorney General that even after the completion of the domestic enquiry the same was forwarded to the highest authority of the B.D.R. in due course for his approval are that consumes time and in the instant case the highest authority approved the dismissal order on 4.2.96 whereupon he was released from his service on that very date vide Annexure 'F' to the petition. 

 12. We have perused the decision relied on by Mr. Hussain and it appears that in that case the service regulation itself embodied a stipulation that if the disciplinary proceeding could not be completed within 180 days at the initiation of the proceeding the accused shall stand discharged after the expiry of 180 days and accused shall be considered to be not guilty of the charges but in the instant case there is nothing in the Ordinance to indicate that in the event of non-compliance with the time limit as embodied in section 6(2) would follow any such consequence. On the otherhands, on a perusal of the decision reported in AIR 1980(SC) it appears that the difference between a mandatory rule and a directory rule is that while the former must be strictly observed, in the case of the latter, substantial compliance may be sufficient to achieve the object regarding when which the rule is enacted. 

 13. In the instant case we have already found that failure of non-compliance of the time limit as contemplated by section 6(2) of the Ordinance did not cause any serious prejudice to the petitioner nor the same led to any consequence which cause prejudice to the petitioner. 

 15. It cannot be doubted that for the purpose of deciding whether reinstatement has to be ordered the court will have to consider the circumstances of a particular case and the nature of the misconduct alleged on the part of the employee as also the nature of contravention of any provision of law. In our opinion, it cannot be the object of the Ordinance that notwithstanding the fact that the sepoy who has been found guilty in a proper domestic enquiry and punished for such misconduct, has to be given relief when once he has shown that the order of punishment was passed beyond the period of twenty days referred to in section 6(2) of the Ordinance. Such a position is not warranted by the statute. Nor will it be conducive to discipline and the cordial relationships that should exist between the employer and employee. 

 17. The provisions as contained in sections 4 and 6 of the Ordinance only emphasis that competent authoriting should be vigilant in taking disciplinary action against a jawan for misconduct, once the said misconduct has come to his notice and that, as far as possible the proceedings including the final orders imposing punishment should be completed within the period. Much emphasis has been laid by Mr. Hossain that the expression used in section 6(2) of the Ordinance is "shall" and that there is no indication in the section enabling the court to take into account any other extraneous matters. According to the learned Advocate the use of the expression "shall" complied with the clear working of the section, clearly shows that the provision is mandatory and not directory. But, in our opinion, that is not the way to interpret a provision in the statute. On the other hand, the relevant provision will have to be construed in the context in which they appear and having due regard to the objects which are sought to be served by the Act in question. 

 18. Here it may be mentioned that there can be no controversy that an employee is entitled to a fair and reasonable opportunity of pleading to the charge for which he may be tried by the domestic tribunal. Does it mean that when orders of punishment for misconducts are passed by an authority after holding a proper and fair enquiry, these orders will have to be set aside, only on the ground that on the day when they were passed, the period of twenty days had already passed? If the contention of Mr. Hussain is accepted, the position will be that even though very serious misconduct is held to be proved against an employee and he does not deserve to be retained in service, nevertheless the order of punishment will be straight way be set aside on the ground that the period of twenty days has expired. The employee will then straightway get back into service however undesirable he may be. The object of section 6(2) of the Ordinance is only to emphasis that the BDR authority should act diligently and with all possible speal and without Itches in the matter of taking action for misconduct against a "member" and passing suitable orders. For all the foregoing reasons we hold that the provision of time limit as embodied in sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Ordinance is not mandatory and is simply directory. Thus we find force and substance in the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney General that fixation of time limit in section 6(2) of the Ordinance is directory and not mandatory and that non-compliance with that provision does not afford a cause of action to the petitioner in a court of law.
